title: Produce, don't possess
hookLine: the Tao gives birth and nourishes, but doesn't possess (Tao Te Ching 51)

cards: A parent at the curb on the first day of school waves, and then drives away. A week of chapters ends today, and under all of them runs one quiet thread: less grabbing. Great skill that looks clumsy.
Knowing what is enough. Knowing the world without going out the door. Subtracting a little each day.

A mind with no fixed position. A traveler with no handhold for the tiger. Chapter fifty-one takes that thread to the very source of things, and asks what the Tao itself does with everything it brings to life.
The answer sounds a lot like that wave at the curb.

teach.h: ALL THINGS COME FROM THE TAO.
teach.b: First, the making. All things come from the Tao, the chapter says, and are nourished by its virtue, its power, the Te in Tao Te Ching. Then they take shape and are brought to completion.
Things grow, in this picture, because something gives and keeps on giving. Second, the honor. Everything honors the Tao, but not because anyone ordered it to.
Nobody issues a decree. The respect simply arises, the way people come to trust a well that has never run dry. Third, the line that gives today its title.
In James Legge's translation: "It produces them and makes no claim to the possession of them." And it keeps going in the same rhythm. It carries things along and doesn't boast.
It brings them to maturity and doesn't control them. The chapter calls this the mysterious virtue. The source gives life, and then lets go of what it gave life to.
Fourth, closer to home. Making something and wanting to own it can arrive as a single motion. The project with your name on it.
The kid who should turn out the way you planned. The friend you helped, who ought to remember. The chapter doesn't say stop making, stop raising, stop helping.

teach.h: MAKE IT FULLY, THEN DON'T HOLD THE DEED.
teach.b: It says do all of it, fully, and then don't hold the deed.
A garden grows better when the gardener stops pulling up the seedlings to check the roots.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-one as a model for parents, teachers and leaders: give fully, nourish, and then let what you helped become its own.

o: to make as much as you can, as fast as you can
to grow crops and vegetables to sell at market
to give life to something without claiming to own it

s: chapter fifty-one says the Tao controls what it brings to maturity
it says the opposite: it brings things to maturity and doesn't control them.
the chapter says all things honor the Tao without being ordered to
nobody issues a decree; the honor simply arises.
the chapter tells people to stop making things
it pictures a source that produces fully and then lets go of what it made.

games.q: you're the source in chapter fifty-one. you've given life to something and seen it grow. what now?
o: let it go and don't boast.
games.why: the Tao produces things and makes no claim to own them, carries them along without boasting, and brings them to maturity without control.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've helped along lately: a plant, a project, a younger colleague, a child.
See it as it is now, a little further on than before, and notice any wish to steer it, to be thanked, to have it turn out your way.
You don't have to push that wish away; just set it down beside you for these two minutes, and let the thing you helped be its own.

wordCard.voice: Produce. In chapter fifty-one, the Tao produces all things and makes no claim to own them. It gives life, and doesn't grab what it gave. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: it gives life and does not possess, from chapter fifty-one.

carryVoice: Your line: don't possess. Full giving, then open hands, the way the source does it. That's the week.
